title: Cities across US oppose Trump FCC plan to preempt local broadband rules
gist: The FCC under Chairman Brendan Carr is using Title II authority it otherwise opposes to propose preempting local broadband permitting rules with a 120-day approval deadline and capped fees, a move cable/telco lobbies support but that mayors, counties, and city groups call illegal federal overreach that ignores ISP-caused delays like permit-hoarding; reply comments are due November 5, with litigation likely if the FCC finalizes the rule.

insights.claim: The FCC's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking would establish a rebuttable presumption that state and local governments have effectively prohibited wireline telecommunications deployment if they fail to process rights-of-way authorizations within 120 days, and would limit fees to a 'reasonable approximation' of a government's actual direct right-of-way management costs via proposed 'safe harbor' fee levels not yet finalized.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A binding 120-day federal deadline plus fee caps would materially reduce local governments' negotiating leverage over broadband infrastructure deployment, directly benefiting large ISPs' capex planning and speed-to-market while removing a local revenue source.
insights.quote: establish a rebuttable presumption that state and local governments have effectively prohibited the provision of wireline telecommunications services
insights.locator: The FCC said its preemption plan would

insights.claim: The FCC claims authority to preempt local rules under Section 253 of the Communications Act (part of Title II), arguing that infrastructure deployed by broadband providers is used for 'both telecommunications and non-telecommunications services' even though FCC Chairman Brendan Carr has consistently opposed classifying broadband itself as a Title II telecommunications service.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A notable legal inconsistency — Carr's FCC invoking Title II authority for preemption while rejecting Title II classification of broadband itself for net neutrality purposes — creates a clear opening for legal challenge on regulatory-authority grounds.
insights.locator: FCC Chairman Brendan Carr has consistently opposed Title II regulation

insights.claim: A joint filing by the United States Conference of Mayors, National Association of Counties, National League of Cities, and National Association of Telecommunications Officers and Advisors argued local permitting is an essential public safety function, not a barrier, and that coordinating safe deployment of wireline infrastructure in public rights-of-way cannot be reduced to an arbitrary federal deadline.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A broad, unified coalition of major local-government associations opposing the rule signals significant organized political and likely litigation resistance if the FCC finalizes the proposal, raising implementation risk/delay for ISPs counting on faster permitting.
insights.quote: Local permitting is not a barrier to broadband deployment—it is an essential public safety function protecting residents, taxpayers, and all users of finite, multi-tenant public rights-of-way.
insights.locator: “Local permitting is not a barrier to broadband deployment

insights.claim: Local government groups pointed out that federal agencies like the Bureau of Land Management and US Forest Service have a 270-day deadline (with no consequence for missing it) for processing wireless/fiber permits on federal property, arguing this shows the FCC's proposed 120-day deadline for local governments is 'arbitrary and bears no connection to the realities of permitting processes.'
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A sharp comparative data point (270 days for federal agencies vs. 120 days demanded of local governments) undercuts the FCC's stated rationale and strengthens the legal/political case that the rule singles out local governments unfairly.
insights.quote: arbitrary and bears no connection to the realities of permitting processes and procedures
insights.locator: The federal standard of 270 days shows

insights.claim: Local governments urged the FCC to instead address provider-caused delays, alleging ISPs engage in 'permit-hoarding' — claiming pole or structure space through permits or make-ready-work requests without actual intent or ability to deploy in a timely fashion — which crowds out competitors and forces cities to make capacity decisions based on false assumptions that a permitted provider will deploy soon.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Reframes the deployment-delay narrative: local governments argue ISPs themselves, not permitting bureaucracy, are the primary bottleneck via anticompetitive permit-hoarding, a counter-narrative investors should weigh when assessing which party bears more responsibility for slow broadband buildout.
insights.locator: “We ask the commission to address provider delays

insights.claim: Local government groups proposed the FCC instead require ISPs to deploy networks within 180 days of receiving local authorization, shifting accountability toward providers rather than municipalities.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A concrete counter-proposal (180-day provider deployment mandate) that could become an alternative regulatory framework if adopted, shifting compliance burden onto ISPs instead of cities.
insights.locator: The groups representing local governments urged the FCC

insights.claim: The League of California Cities argued the FCC has no authority to adopt the proposal, asserting that federal preemption of traditional state and local authority over public property and rights-of-way management should require clear congressional authorization, which Congress has not expressly provided.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Sets up the core legal challenge theory (lack of clear congressional authorization) likely to be argued in court if the FCC finalizes the rule, a key factor for assessing litigation risk and timeline to implementation.
insights.quote: Federal preemption of traditional state and local authority over public property, construction, public safety, permitting, and rights-of-way management should rest on clear congressional authorization.
insights.locator: Another filing submitted by the League of California Cities

insights.claim: A filing by Minnesota cities argued the current FCC is repeating a mistake from the first Trump administration, when its attempt to preempt state net neutrality laws was blocked in court, because without Title II regulation of broadband providers the FCC can't convert a 'federal policy of nonregulation into independent preemptive authority.'
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Cites a direct legal precedent (blocked first-Trump-administration net neutrality preemption attempt) suggesting a real risk of the current proposal being similarly struck down in court, informing expectations about the rule's durability if finalized.
insights.locator: A filing by Minnesota cities said the current FCC

insights.claim: Cable and telecom lobby groups support the FCC's plan and want even shorter deadlines: America's Communications Association wants 120 days as an 'outer bound' with 45-day deadlines for 'simple' permits, while USTelecom urged fee limits and said 60- and 90-day deadlines would give cities and towns enough review time.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Shows the ISP lobby is pushing for even more aggressive deadlines than the FCC's proposal, indicating the eventual rule (if adopted) could tighten further in the ISPs' favor during the rulemaking process, a key thing for investors in broadband providers to track.
insights.locator: The cable lobby group said 120 days should be an “outer bound”

insights.claim: FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in June that some jurisdictions cause lengthy delays, excessive fees, and unpredictable permitting that can postpone projects for months or years, and floated giving ISPs 'incentives' to build faster rather than imposing new legal requirements on them, while Democratic Commissioner Anna Gomez voted to open the proceeding to comment but signaled she would vote against the final rule, questioning the FCC's Section 253 authority.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Confirms a partisan split on the commission (Carr pushing the plan, Gomez opposing) that signals the final rule, if it passes, will likely be along party lines and face a dissenting commissioner's legal objections as further ammunition for litigation.
insights.quote: I am dubious about the commission’s authority under Section 253 to use rulemaking to preempt states and localities
insights.locator: Democratic Commissioner Anna Gomez approved the step

insights.claim: The first round of public comments closed the day before this article was published, with reply comments due to the FCC by November 5, 2026, after which the FCC would finalize new rules, assuming it doesn't drop the proposal entirely.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Gives investors and stakeholders a concrete near-term regulatory timeline (November 5, 2026 reply comment deadline) to watch for the next procedural step toward a final rule.
insights.locator: The deadline for the first round of comments passed yesterday
